items.title: Locally Robust Inference with Outcomes Predicted by Machine Learning
items.desc: Develops a three-step debiased GMM framework that gives valid inference when the dependent variable is itself generated by a machine learning model, and applies it to U.S. mortgage data. The race-blind ML default-risk score predicts default well, but the conditional Black–White disparity embedded in the score is much smaller than the disparity in realized serious delinquency. [arXiv econ.EM, submitted 2026-10-15]

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Welcome back. Today's paper is about a quiet problem in empirical economics: what happens when the outcome variable you analyze was itself predicted by a machine learning model.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: That's very common now. Researchers use satellite images or text to build measures of consumption, or predict long-run earnings from short-run proxies, and then treat that predicted number as if it were observed.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Right, and the paper's point is that this threatens valid inference, because the first-step estimation error and any model-selection bias leak into the second step. The author, who writes from the Bank of Spain, builds a three-step locally robust method of moments estimator.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: In plain terms, the idea is to add correction terms, called influence functions, for both the first and second estimation steps. That makes the final estimate locally insensitive to regularization and model-selection mistakes in the machine learning stages.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: The paper shows the estimator is consistent and asymptotically normal, and checks finite-sample behavior with Monte Carlo simulations. It lists settings where this applies, like dynamic treatment effects, long-term effects with surrogates, and productivity estimation with constructed instruments.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: Then there's the empirical application, on U.S. mortgage data. The question is whether a race-blind machine learning default-risk score still embeds racial disparities, conditional on other characteristics.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: The score predicts later default well overall. But the conditional Black–White disparity inside the score is much smaller than the disparity in realized serious delinquency. And when you account for first-step estimation, the naive out-of-sample estimate of the score disparity goes up.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: So one caveat is that this is a methods paper first; the application illustrates the tool rather than settling the fairness debate. Takeaway: if your outcome was predicted by a model, your standard errors need to know that.

items.title: Algorithmic Collusion Without Deterrence: Auditing the Punishment Mechanism in Q-Learning Pricing Agents
items.desc: Replicates the Calvano et al. Q-learning Bertrand duopoly and audits frozen policies, finding that the apparent reward-punishment pattern does not identify a deterrence mechanism: in 914 of 1,024 converged pairs a single attractor covers the whole state space. Re-matching frozen agents from independent runs cuts coordination by 80%, and the optimal deviation would profit by 17.5% on average. [arXiv q-fin.CP, submitted 2026-10-15]

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Today: a paper asking whether AI pricing algorithms that seem to collude actually punish each other for cheating. It's going to the ACM conference on AI in Finance in Milan.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: The backdrop is a well-known result. Simple Q-learning agents repricing in a duopoly end up charging supracompetitive prices, and the classic study read that as a learned reward-punishment scheme: undercut your rival and it retaliates.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: That reading matters for regulators, because high prices defended by retaliation look like a cartel. So these authors replicate the original environment and confirm the impulse-response pattern within co-trained pairs. A forced price cut leads to a drop, and then prices return.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: Then they audit with learning switched off, on frozen policies. And the pattern turns out not to identify a mechanism. In nine of ten converged pairs, 914 of 1,024, one attractor's basin is the entire state space, so every perturbation just returns to the same place.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: They even show that a forced price increase triggers the same so-called retaliation as an undercut. That's not selective punishment; it's just a system that always snaps back.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: Another finding: coordination is specific to the pair. If you re-match frozen agents from independent training runs, coordination collapses by eighty percent.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: And the incentive accounting is striking. The one-period undercut in the standard test is indeed unprofitable, confirmed in ninety-two percent of pairs. But the optimal deviation, computed by dynamic programming against the partner's frozen strategy, profits by seventeen and a half percent on average.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: So collusion survives because deviation is never tried, not because it wouldn't pay. The caveat is that this is tabular Q-learning in a simulated duopoly. Takeaway: high prices are robust, but the punishment story and remedies built on it deserve a second look.

items.title: Momentum, Commentary Tone, and Earnings Surprise in LLM Financial Forecasts
items.desc: Builds synthetic earnings announcements that independently reverse 20-day momentum, commentary tone and EPS-versus-consensus surprise, and tests six small open language-model checkpoints (0.49–7.61B parameters) with 2,016 prompts each. Tone's effect exceeds EPS surprise in five of six models and momentum exceeds it in five, while the EPS effect ranges from −0.19 to 86.80 percentage points. [arXiv cs.LG, submitted 2026-10-15]

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Today's paper asks a simple question about language models in finance: when an LLM forecasts a stock reaction to earnings, what is it actually paying attention to?

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: In real announcements, momentum, upbeat wording and an earnings beat usually move together, so you can't separate them. This study builds synthetic announcements where each one is reversed independently.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Concretely, they hold actual earnings per share fixed and flip the surprise by changing the stated consensus, while separately reversing twenty-day price momentum and the tone of the commentary.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: They test six small open model checkpoints from four families, from about half a billion to 7.6 billion parameters, with 2,016 prompts each. Answer labels are reversed too, to rule out simple answer-order preferences.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: The headline: the effect of the earnings surprise ranges from basically nothing, minus 0.19 percentage points, to nearly 87 points, depending on the model. In five of six models, the effect of the tone of commentary is larger than the effect of the EPS surprise, and momentum beats it in five as well.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: A separate diagnostic asks the models directly whether earnings beat consensus, using natural-word numbers. Accuracy there ranges from 51 percent, basically chance, to 95.8 percent.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: The author is careful about limits. These are shifts in answer scores, not calibrated market probabilities, and momentum reliance isn't necessarily wrong since price history can be informative. It shows neither an internal reasoning mechanism nor real return predictability.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: Takeaway: before trusting a small LLM's financial forecast, check whether it reads the numbers or just the mood.

briefing.speaker: A
briefing.text: Hello and welcome to the AI research digest for October sixteenth, twenty twenty-six. I'm Alex.

briefing.speaker: B
briefing.text: And I'm Sam. Today's theme is a nervous market: papers on how AI systems behave in finance, and a lot of news about the AI trade wobbling.

briefing.speaker: A
briefing.text: Let's start with research. A new arXiv paper looks at how language models forecast reactions to earnings announcements. The author built synthetic announcements, and flipped momentum, commentary tone and the earnings surprise independently.

briefing.speaker: A
briefing.text: In five of six small models, the tone of the commentary had a bigger effect than the actual earnings surprise, and momentum did too. One model barely reacted to the surprise at all. The author is careful that this isn't proof of how the models reason.

briefing.speaker: B
briefing.text: Still, a useful warning for anyone building forecasting tools. Next, a paper on algorithmic collusion. Earlier work found that simple Q-learning pricing agents settle on high prices, and read it as a learned punishment scheme.

briefing.speaker: A
briefing.text: These authors audit that on frozen policies. The punishment pattern turns out to be a system that always snaps back, even after a price increase. And coordination collapses by eighty percent if you pair agents from different training runs.

briefing.speaker: B
briefing.text: So the story that regulators tell about retaliation may be incomplete.

briefing.speaker: A
briefing.text: One more paper, from econometrics. When researchers use a machine learning prediction as their outcome variable, standard errors are wrong. The author proposes a debiased method, and applies it to mortgage data, finding the disparity in a race-blind default score is much smaller than in realized delinquency.

briefing.speaker: B
briefing.text: Now the news. The big story is the sell-off in AI infrastructure. The New York Times and Bloomberg both cover the wipeout in so-called neocloud companies like CoreWeave, with investors worried about borrowing costs as yields climb.

briefing.speaker: A
briefing.text: The Financial Times reports investors dumping data centre bonds, with AI borrowers facing a Darwin moment. And the Wall Street Journal says CoreWeave shows a pressure point from higher rates.

briefing.speaker: B
briefing.text: Yet demand signals remain strong. Bloomberg reports that Schneider Electric raised its outlook again on data-center demand, with visibility stretching into twenty twenty-eight.

briefing.speaker: A
briefing.text: The Wall Street Journal also reports Anthropic's quarterly revenue jumped forty-five percent to nearly seventeen billion dollars, as the company met investors ahead of its planned IPO next month.

briefing.speaker: B
briefing.text: Two policy items. Bloomberg says China proposed export controls on advanced AI technologies, including models and chip designs. And the Financial Times says G7 economies plan simulated AI attacks on banks.

briefing.speaker: A
briefing.text: Finally, the Wall Street Journal on how insurance could become AI's next obstacle, given potential multibillion-dollar liabilities, and how AI agents are creating headaches for online sellers.

briefing.speaker: B
briefing.text: That's the digest for today. Find the full archive and the paper explainers on the web archive linked in your email. Thanks for listening.
